# Joint-stock company and limited liability (`joint_stock_company`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/economy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Economy & finance (`economy`)
- Deps: helped by partnership_commenda, double_entry, rule_of_law, stock_exchange
- Core idea: The capital is divided into many equal shares that can be sold to others; the company is a legal person that owns property, signs contracts and outlives its members; shareholders elect directors and receive dividends out of profit; with limited liability a shareholder can lose his stake but no more. This locks capital into long ventures (ships, mines, canals, railways) while each investor can still get out by selling his share instead of withdrawing money from the firm. Minimum design: a charter or general law of incorporation, a share register, audited accounts shown to shareholders, and dividends paid only from profit.
- Pitfalls:
  - Limited liability without disclosure or audit invites swindles and bubbles (South Sea Company 1720)
  - Forgetting that managers spend other people's money (Adam Smith's complaint): owners need votes, accounts and the power to dismiss
  - Paying dividends out of capital to keep the share price up: a classic fraud
  - Saying the Dutch East India Company was the first company: Roman tax-farming societies and the Toulouse mill companies had shares centuries earlier
  - Tying incorporation to a royal monopoly charter: it becomes a favour for courtiers rather than a tool for anyone
- History: rome: 2nd–1st c. BC – societates publicanorum, tax-farming companies with shares (partes) held by outside investors; how freely shares were traded is disputed; europe: 12th c. – mill owners at Toulouse hold transferable shares (uchaux), consolidated in 1372 into the Bazacle company, which lasted until 1946; 1407 Genoa's Casa di San Giorgio with tradable shares in public debt; 1555 Muscovy Company charter; 1600 English East India Company; 1602 Dutch VOC with permanent capital (from 1612) and shares traded in Amsterdam; 1720 Bubble Act; 1855–1856 British general limited liability; islamic: 1775 – Ottoman esham, shares in the revenue of tax farms sold to the public; china: 1872 – China Merchants' Steam Navigation Company pools merchant share capital under official supervision; east_asia: 1873 – First National Bank of Japan, founded by Shibusawa Eiichi as a joint-stock company; americas: 1811 – New York general incorporation act for manufacturing firms with limited liability
- Read:
  - Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (1776), book V ch. 1
  - William N. Goetzmann & K. Geert Rouwenhorst (eds.), The Origins of Value (2005)
  - John Micklethwait & Adrian Wooldridge, The Company: A Short History of a Revolutionary Idea (2003)
